POL.title: Chapels carved from salt
POL.body: Mining at Wieliczka and Bochnia began in the 1200s. Over the centuries, miners turned part of the underground workings into chapels, sculptures and galleries carved into the salt itself. The result is both an industrial landscape and an extraordinary subterranean art collection.

CHN.title: A sacred mountain and a scientific instrument
CHN.body: At Dengfeng, temples stand alongside a sundial platform and an observatory. Buildings accumulated over nine dynasties around a mountain regarded as the center of heaven and earth: measuring the sky and interpreting it spiritually were part of the same landscape.

CHN.title: A town organized around water
CHN.body: Lijiang grew into an important trading town on uneven ground. Its builders fitted streets and buildings to the terrain while developing an intricate water-supply network, an engineering achievement that became part of the town's distinctive form.

IND.title: An imperial monument to grief
IND.body: Shah Jahan ordered the Taj Mahal built as a memorial to his wife. The marble mausoleum took shape in Agra between 1631 and 1648, turning a private bereavement into one of the Mughal Empire's most ambitious architectural projects.

AFG.title: A crossroads preserved in a cliff
AFG.body: Bamiyan's monasteries and sanctuaries brought different artistic traditions together in Buddhist Gandhara art. Later Islamic fortifications added another layer to the valley's history. The Taliban destroyed its two monumental standing Buddhas in March 2001; the wider archaeological landscape preserves much more than their empty niches.

IDN.title: A pilgrimage built in tiers
IDN.body: Borobudur was built in Java in the eighth and ninth centuries. A visitor ascends from square terraces to circular platforms ringed by 72 perforated stupas, each sheltering a Buddha. Its carved reliefs cover roughly 2,500 square meters, making the ascent a journey through imagery as well as architecture.

ETH.title: Churches excavated from the mountain
ETH.body: At Lalibela, medieval builders carved eleven churches directly from rock. This thirteenth-century sacred landscape was conceived as a New Jerusalem. Creating a building meant removing stone around and inside it, rather than assembling walls from separate blocks.

MLI.title: Gold trade and flood engineering
MLI.body: Djenné linked inland markets to the gold trade across the Sahara. Its traditional houses were raised on small mounds called toguere, adapting a prosperous trading town to seasonal flooding. Commerce and the rhythm of the river shaped the same city.

GRC.title: An island city turned fortress
GRC.body: The Knights of St John occupied Rhodes from 1309 to 1523 and rebuilt it as a fortified stronghold. Ottoman rule later added mosques and baths among the Gothic buildings. Walking through the old town reveals successive rulers through the structures they left behind.

MAR.title: A fortress made of earth
MAR.body: At Ait-Ben-Haddou, houses cluster behind defensive walls and corner towers, all built in the earthen architectural tradition of southern Morocco. The fortified settlement shows how a community could create monumental defenses from the same material as its homes.

GTM.title: A city beneath the forest
GTM.body: Tikal's temples rise above the Guatemalan forest, but they were once only the ceremonial core of a much larger Maya settlement. Palaces, public squares and ramps connected this center, while homes extended into the surrounding countryside. Occupation spanned roughly the sixth century BCE to the tenth century CE.

PAK.title: A capital remembered through its tombs
PAK.body: Thatta served three successive dynasties before coming under Mughal rule. From the fourteenth through eighteenth centuries, rulers and patrons embellished the city and its enormous burial landscape at Makli. The monuments preserve changing ambitions and artistic traditions long after the courts themselves disappeared.

PHL.title: Mountains redesigned for rice
PHL.body: Ifugao communities turned steep mountain contours into irrigated rice terraces. Maintaining the landscape depends on knowledge passed between generations and coordinated work across a community. These fields are an enduring piece of agricultural engineering, rather than simply a picturesque view.

AUS.title: An archive written on rock
AUS.body: Kakadu's paintings, engravings and archaeological sites record an exceptionally long history of life in northern Australia. They preserve evidence of changing techniques and ways of living across tens of thousands of years, within a landscape that remains connected to Aboriginal communities.

IRN.title: The bricks that were never used
IRN.body: Tchogha Zanbil was founded around 1250 BCE as a sacred city of Elam, enclosed by three rings of walls. An invasion by Ashurbanipal interrupted its development. Thousands of unused bricks left at the site give unusually tangible evidence of a building project that never reached completion.

KHM.title: An entire landscape of capitals
KHM.body: Angkor Wat is only one part of Angkor. The archaeological park covers about 400 square kilometers and preserves successive capitals of the Khmer Empire from the ninth to fifteenth centuries, including Angkor Thom and its richly carved Bayon temple. The famous towers belonged to a much larger urban world.

ZWE.title: A medieval trading city in stone
ZWE.body: Great Zimbabwe developed into an important trading center between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries. Its ruins spread across nearly 80 hectares, preserving the scale of a major Shona city and a reminder that medieval commercial networks extended deep into southern Africa.

DZA.title: A port that changed empires
DZA.body: Tipasa began as a Punic trading post on the Mediterranean. Rome captured it and used it as a base for expansion into Mauretania. Phoenician, Roman, early Christian and Byzantine remains now sit alongside local royal monuments, making the coast an unusually compact record of successive worlds.

GBR.title: An observatory designed by two polymaths
GBR.body: The old Royal Observatory at Greenwich was the work of architect Christopher Wren and scientist Robert Hooke. Nearby royal and naval buildings placed astronomy within a wider landscape of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century scientific and artistic ambition.

TUR.title: Monuments before pottery
TUR.body: Hunter-gatherers erected Göbekli Tepe's monumental stone enclosures between about 9600 and 8200 BCE. Their T-shaped pillars carry carvings of wild animals. Built before pottery became part of local life, the structures challenge the idea that monumental architecture required an established farming city.
